analysis.one_liner: Restores legal protections against pension cuts for retirees in troubled union pension plans, funded by taxes on large real estate swaps and huge retirement accounts.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced with 10 senators backing it, was sent to the Senate Finance Committee in May 2017 and never received a hearing, vote, or further action before Congress ended in January 2019.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would undo a 2014 change that allowed certain multiemployer pension plans — pensions run jointly by unions and groups of employers — to cut benefits already promised to retirees. It would let more of these struggling plans get a federal rescue: the Pension Benefit Guaranty Corporation, the government agency that backstops pensions, could take over paying a floor of benefits for plans headed toward insolvency. To pay for it, the bill raises revenue by limiting a tax break on real estate swaps (known as like-kind exchanges), ends that break for art and collectibles, and forces people with more than $5 million in retirement accounts to stop contributing and start withdrawing. It also moves pension debts to the front of the line when an employer goes bankrupt.
analysis.who_benefits: Retirees and active workers in financially troubled multiemployer pension plans — typically union members in industries like trucking, mining, and manufacturing whose plans have more retirees than contributing workers. The bill would bar their plans from cutting already-earned benefits and would create a path for the federal pension insurer to pay a guaranteed floor of benefits when a plan is collapsing. Retirees would also gain when a bankrupt employer's remaining assets go first to pension debts.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Retirees in failing union pension plans

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the 2014 provision that let deeply underfunded multiemployer plans suspend or cut benefits that participants had already earned [S2][S3].

Expands eligibility for PBGC 'partitions,' in which the federal pension insurer takes over paying guaranteed-level benefits for troubled plans, and requires a supplemental payment so partitioned retirees receive up to 80% of the single-employer guarantee [S3].
Creates a dedicated 'legacy fund,' financed by the bill's new tax revenue, to cover the cost of those rescues [S2][S3].

Gives pension withdrawal liabilities first priority among claims in bankruptcy, so when an employer that owes a pension plan liquidates, retirement obligations are paid ahead of other creditors [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Investors who use tax-deferred like-kind exchanges of real estate would pay tax on gains above $1 million per year; art and collectibles would no longer qualify for the exchange break at all; and people with more than $5 million across their retirement accounts could not keep contributing tax-advantaged money and would have to withdraw the excess. In bankruptcies, other creditors — lenders and trade creditors — would rank behind pension debts and recover less.
analysis.who_pays_short: Real estate investors, collectibles traders, very wealthy retirees

drawbacks.text: The rescue is not free: costs that exceed the dedicated legacy fund are paid from the PBGC's general multiemployer insurance fund, which could strain the agency's ability to backstop other failing plans [S3].

The tax changes fall on specific asset classes — large real estate investors and collectibles holders — who argue that limiting like-kind exchanges reduces transaction activity and property values in commercial real estate, a cost that could partly land on workers in that industry [S3].

Requiring faster withdrawals from retirement accounts over $5 million would force very wealthy savers to sell assets and pay tax sooner; supporters call that closing a loophole, but it does change long-standing treatment of large accounts [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is concrete: retirees who earned pensions over long careers would not see those checks cut, and the bill pays for the rescue with tax changes aimed at the largest real estate and retirement-account holders. The honest costs are that the federal pension insurer takes on substantial new liabilities whose funding depends on the new tax revenue holding up, and that the bankruptcy-priority change shifts losses onto other creditors. On balance the bill transfers risk from rank-and-file retirees to high-end asset holders and the pension insurance system.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate sent it to the Finance Committee the day it was introduced, and no hearing, markup, or floor vote ever happened; it died there when the two-year Congress ended in January 2019.

narrative.text: Senator Bernie Sanders introduced the bill on May 9, 2017, joined by nine Democratic cosponsors including Sherrod Brown, Tammy Baldwin, and Amy Klobuchar [S1][S4].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance on the day of introduction — the only action ever taken on the bill [S1][S5].
The Finance Committee took no further action, and the bill never reached the Senate floor before the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019 [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Retirees in failing multiemployer plans got no relief. The parties that benefit from the outcome are large real estate and collectibles investors and holders of $5 million-plus retirement accounts, who keep the tax treatment the bill would have curtailed, and employers and creditors whose pension obligations keep ranking behind other claims in bankruptcy.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Large investors and creditors; retirees got nothing

for.name: Bernie Sanders
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and led its sponsorship.

for.name: 9 Senate Democrats
for.role: Cosponsors (Baldwin, Brown, Franken, Klobuchar, McCaskill, Peters, Reed, Stabenow, Whitehouse)

against.name: Senate Finance Committee (Republican-controlled)
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Sen. Orrin Hatch (R-UT)
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral — no hearing, no markup — leaving it to die at the end of the Congress.

against.name: Senate Republican majority
against.role: Majority party controlling the Senate floor and agenda
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the floor; with the committee inactive, the bill never advanced.

sides.party_line_note: All ten sponsors were Democrats or the Independent caucusing with them; no Republican supported it, and the bill died in a committee controlled by Republicans.

industries.industry: Retirees and workers in multiemployer (union) pension plans
industries.note: These are the bill's intended beneficiaries: their earned benefits would be protected from cuts and backstopped by a federal rescue when their plans fail. Millions of union workers in trucking, mining, and manufacturing have retirement security riding on whether these plans survive.

The bill would cap the like-kind exchange deferral at $1 million of gain per year, ending unlimited tax deferral on large property swaps. Their tax savings come at the cost of the pension funding the bill provides.
Collectibles would be excluded from like-kind exchange treatment entirely, removing a tax advantage for high-end art and collectibles trading.

industries.industry: Households with over $5 million in retirement accounts
industries.note: The bill would bar further contributions to such accounts and require accelerated withdrawals, ending unlimited tax-sheltered accumulation for the wealthiest retirement savers.
Pension withdrawal liabilities would jump to first priority in bankruptcy, so lenders and other creditors of failing employers would recover less when a company that owes a pension plan goes under.

industries.industry: Pension Benefit Guaranty Corporation (federal pension insurer)
industries.note: The agency would gain a dedicated legacy fund and clearer procedures, but would also take on substantial new long-term benefit obligations, with any shortfall falling on its general multiemployer fund that backstops other plans.
